title: Bellarmine De Justif. 1.7 summarizes apprehension, double assent, faith vs science
source_text: XXIX. Quae omnia satis aperte tradita reperiuntur apud Bellarminum capite illo septimo jam citato, ubi diserte monet in eo qui credit duo esse, apprehensionem, & judicium sive assensum, quamvis ejus apprehensio non sit fides, sed aliquid fidem praecedens. Deinde apprehensionem non dici proprie notitiam, si sit rudis & confusa, qualis reperitur in fidelibus rusticis: distinctam autem & perspicuam, qualis est Theologi, vel Philosophi, non necessario requiri ad fidem. Ac praeterea distinguit duplicem assensum, unum qui sequitur rationem & evidentiam rei, alterum qui sequitur authoritatem proponentis, & vult priorem tantum dici notitiam, si proprie loqui velimus; posteriorem vero assensum dici fidem; juxta illud Augustini, Quod intelligimus aliquid, rationi debemus; quod autem credimus, authoritati. Unde colligit mysteria fidei quae rationem superant credi, non intelligi; ac per hoc fidem a scientia distingui, & hoc respectu melius per ignorantiam quam per scientiam definiri. Ac denique caput illud septimum concludit his verbis: Tametsi distinguatur fides a scientia, tamen utilis est etiam, & laudabilis scientia rerum divinarum, quippe quae amorem Dei semper magis & magis accendit: & sicut laude digni sunt qui discendo proficiunt, ita merito reprehenduntur qui semper discunt, & ad scientiam veritatis nunquam perveniunt.
pass_a_gloss: All of this is found set out clearly enough in Bellarmine in that seventh chapter already cited, where he expressly warns that in the one who believes there are two things, apprehension and judgment or assent, although his apprehension is not faith but something preceding faith. Next, that apprehension is not properly called notitia if it is rude and confused, as found in rustic believers; while distinct and clear notitia, such as belongs to a theologian or philosopher, is not necessarily required for faith. He further distinguishes a double assent, one that follows the reason and evidence of the thing, another that follows the authority of the one proposing, and he wants only the former to be called notitia if we speak properly, while the latter assent is called faith, according to Augustine: what we understand we owe to reason; what we believe, to authority. Hence he gathers that the mysteries of faith which surpass reason are believed, not understood; and by this faith is distinguished from science, and in this respect is better defined through ignorance than through science. Finally that seventh chapter concludes: although faith is distinguished from science, knowledge of divine things is nevertheless also useful and laudable, since it always kindles the love of God more and more; and just as those who advance by learning are praiseworthy, so those who are always learning and never arrive at the knowledge of the truth are rightly blamed.
pass_b_english: Bellarmine De Justif. 1.7 gathers the preceding points: believer has apprehension plus assent; rude rustic apprehension is not properly notitia; distinct theological notitia is not required for faith.

He splits assent into evidence-following (notitia) and authority-following (faith), citing Augustine; mysteries above reason are believed not understood, so faith is better defined by ignorance than science, yet divine science remains useful and laudable.
